name: Canada
law:
▸WHAT THE LAW HERE COUNTS AS ENGINEERED
Trait-based
Regulation attaches to the trait rather than the method. The question is whether the plant or animal has a characteristic that is new or risky; how it was produced does not matter. In principle that catches a risky organism however it was made, conventional breeding included. In practice most gene-edited organisms are waved through, because an edit that could have arisen naturally is not counted as new. Canada is the clearest case, with transgenic events and products of mutagenesis or editing sitting in the same register, which makes it the one place the second group stays visible. Only two countries on this map work this way.
▸DECISIONS FILED TO THE CARTAGENA PROTOCOL
94 decisions filed by this country. A decision is a ruling on whether a living modified organism may be used, imported or released here.

What you can do about this
▸TEST IT YOURSELF6
CFIA laboratories
TESTING
The agency's own laboratory network runs seed and grain analysis for enforcement.
Visit source ↗
EnviroLogix QuickStix
TESTING
Lateral flow strips, the same format as a pregnancy test. Crush tissue or seed in water, dip, read in five to ten minutes. Sold to anyone, a few pounds each, in packs. Strips are trait-specific, so know which trait to look for before buying.
Visit source ↗
Romer Labs AgraStrip
TESTING
Strips plus the extraction kits that go with them, sold internationally — which matters because the trait to test for differs by region.
Visit source ↗
Agdia ImmunoStrip
TESTING
Sells in small quantities with published prices, which makes it the most usable of the three for someone testing a handful of samples rather than a lorry.
Visit source ↗
Eurofins — laboratory GMO testing
TESTING
The largest food and feed testing network in the world, with laboratories in more than 60 countries and the default commercial route for a confirmatory DNA test. A strip result tells you what to do next; this is what an enforcement body acts on.
Visit source ↗
GMOMETHODS — the EU database of validated detection methods, and the ENGL laboratory network
IF YOU ARE COMMISSIONING A TEST, THIS IS WHERE THE METHOD COMES FROM. An application to authorise a GM food or feed in the EU MUST INCLUDE A METHOD FOR DETECTING, IDENTIFYING AND QUANTIFYING IT, and the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL GMFF, hosted by the Joint Research Centre) validates that method for sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and reliability. The validated methods are then PUBLISHED FREE in the GMOMETHODS database, searchable by EVENT, UNIQUE IDENTIFIER, SPECIES, APPLICANT and technique. So for most authorised events anywhere in the world there is a published, peer-validated PCR method a laboratory can be asked to run — and the unique identifier this map keeps telling readers to write down is the key to finding it. The JRC also publishes decision tools, GMO-MATRIX and EVENT-FINDER. Behind it sits the EUROPEAN NETWORK OF GMO LABORATORIES (ENGL), the national enforcement laboratories of every EU country PLUS NORWAY, SWITZERLAND AND TURKEY. THE HONEST LIMIT: detecting UNAUTHORISED GMOs relies on screening that only indicates presence and needs confirmation by other approaches; and the EURL and ENGL's own report of 26 March 2019 addresses the difficulty of detecting organisms made by NEW MUTAGENESIS TECHNIQUES — gene-edited plants may leave nothing a method can target. Work on GM animals and microorganisms is still in progress.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO AUTHORISES A RELEASE4
CFIA — plants with novel traits
REGULATOR
Authorises plants with novel traits and publishes a decision document for each. Canada is one of very few registers listing edited and inserted-gene products side by side, which makes it the best place to check what an organism actually is.
Visit source ↗
Health Canada — novel foods
REGULATOR
Assesses anything sold as food and publishes the decisions.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — national focal points
REGULATOR
Every party to the Cartagena Protocol must name a contact for biosafety, and the list is public. For most of the world it is the only named biosafety contact that exists, and it holds the decisions filed for that country.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — what a country profile holds
Referenced by 135 rows in this box. A country profile on the Clearing-House holds the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO TAKES A COMPLAINT8
Your provincial agriculture ministry
COMPLAINT
The CFIA authorises; the province licenses applicators and takes drift complaints.
Provincial ministries and the federal PMRA — drift complaints
COMPLAINT
Both levels take a drift complaint, and the row is worth knowing because the federal route is the documented one. Provinces and territories licence commercial applicators, vendors and growers, issue permits for certain uses, and enforce their own pest control statutes with inspections, violation tickets and prosecutions. But Health Canada's Pest Management Regulatory Agency also inspects and investigates the sale, importation and use of pesticides through regional officers across the country, and it investigates drift, misapplication and misuse directly. Where the numbers come from, and what they leave out — CCAC, the UK count, and the countries with none
ONLY A HANDFUL OF COUNTRIES COUNT AT ALL, and each counts something different — which is why global totals in this field should be read as estimates. CANADA'S CCAC publishes an annual ANIMAL DATA REPORT with DOWNLOADABLE SORTABLE SPREADSHEETS breaking down species, purpose and INVASIVENESS CATEGORY — the most usable open dataset of its kind. BRITAIN counts every regulated procedure on a protected animal under the ANIMALS (SCIENTIFIC PROCEDURES) ACT 1986, covering all vertebrates AND CEPHALOPODS, published annually by the Home Office, with NORTHERN IRELAND counting separately. THE EXCLUSIONS ARE THE POINT. Canada's CCAC covers only CERTIFIED INSTITUTIONS — typically universities — so most private laboratories and companies are absent unless government-funded, and the CCAC sets no standardised submission method. The US counts only AWA-covered mammals, excluding mice, rats and birds; official figures near 800,000 sit against unofficial estimates of 12–24 million. INVERTEBRATES SUCH AS FRUIT FLIES AND WORMS ARE NOT PROTECTED AND NOT COUNTED ANYWHERE. And JAPAN PUBLISHES NO OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT DATA at all — the only figures come from a professional association survey to which a third of facilities did not respond. Where a country publishes nothing, an estimate is all that exists.
